## Setup


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)
```
:::

---

## The question

Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a
sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a
statement about how wrong it might be.

Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won't.


**In this analysis, I look at median household income across counties in New York, and
ask which communities we measure most and least reliably.**

---

## Choosing what to measure



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
my_state <- "NY"        # two-letter abbreviation, in quotes
my_variable <- "B19013_001"     # the variable code, in quotes
```
:::


## Pulling the data


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
county_data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = my_variable,
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5"
)
```
:::


Let's look at what came back.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
dim(county_data)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

```


:::


**[How many rows did you get? Does that match the number of counties in your state?]**

---

## How big is the margin of error?

A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000
than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a
percentage.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)
```
:::


Now sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}


Hamilton County has the largest margin of error relative to its estimate and its 10.925308.
---

## Sorting counties into reliability categories


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 10 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

count(county_data, reliability)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  reliability         n
  <chr>           <int>
1 High confidence    53
2 Low confidence      1
3 Moderate            8
```


:::
:::




**[How many counties fall into each category?]**
There are 53 counties counties in high confidence, 1 county in low confidence and 8 counties in moderate.
---

## Is the margin of error bigger in small places?

To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row.
That means a **wide** pull.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                         myvarE myvarM    popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                         <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 36001 Albany County, New York       83149   1788  315374    NA
2 36003 Allegany County, New York     61233   2429   47027    NA
3 36005 Bronx County, New York        49036    872 1419250    NA
4 36007 Broome County, New York       61059   1769  197738    NA
5 36009 Cattaraugus County, New York  58248   1978   76479    NA
6 36011 Cayuga County, New York       66583   2266   75464    NA
```


:::
:::




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 15 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))
```
:::


Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 2 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         53        369308.
2 Moderate                 9         33224.
```


:::
:::



**[What is the average population of high-confidence counties versus low-confidence
counties? Is there a pattern?]**
The average population for for high-confidence counties is 369307.62 versus the moderate which is 33223.89. Yes, there is pattern - counties with larger population have high confidence while counties with lower population have low-confidence.
